name: Planor
tagline: All-in-one workspace for agencies and small teams: clients, projects, tasks, time and invoicing in one place.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The individual pieces here are boring CRUD: a clients table, a projects table, tasks with statuses, a timer, and an invoice PDF. An agent can absolutely produce a working single-user version of all five in a weekend, and for a solo freelancer that is often enough. The gap is breadth and glue: the paid product's value is that invoicing knows about tracked time, that a client portal exists, that permissions keep contractors out of the finance tab, and that someone else maintains the whole surface. Multiply that by a team and you are now running internal software instead of billing hours. Verdict is kinda: great for one person, thin the moment a second person logs in.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you add clients, create projects with tasks, run a timer against tasks, and generate an invoice PDF from unbilled time.
requirements: Node 20 and a local machine or small VPS
A place to store SQLite that gets backed up
Optional SMTP credentials if you want to email invoices
whatYouLose: Multi-user roles and permissions, so no hiding revenue from contractors
A client-facing portal for approvals, files and invoice payment
Payment collection: Stripe checkout, reminders, dunning, reconciliation
Mobile apps and offline time tracking, plus notifications that actually arrive
Someone else fixing the calendar edge cases, tax fields and export formats you did not think about
moatNotes: Once your invoice history and client records live somewhere, moving is a project, not a decision.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because agency ops software is only worth anything when everyone uses it, and everyone only uses it when it is fast, mobile, permissioned and never loses a timer entry. A weekend build gives you the data model; the paid product gives you a thing your account manager will actually open on a Tuesday, plus invoices that clients can pay without a phone call. Also, billing is the one place where a bug costs real money, and most people would rather that bug be someone else's problem.
notes: Solo freelancers can genuinely self-host this; the moment you hire, the DIY version starts costing more in maintenance than the seats did.
prompt:
Build a single-user agency operations app called "Shop" that runs entirely on my machine.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, schema and migrations with Drizzle ORM
- Tailwind CSS, no component library
- Server Actions for all mutations, no separate API layer
- pdf-lib for invoice PDF generation

Data model:
- clients: name, email, address, hourly_rate, notes
- projects: client_id, name, status (active/paused/done), budget_hours
- tasks: project_id, title, status (todo/doing/done), estimate_hours, due_date
- time_entries: task_id, started_at, ended_at, minutes, billable (bool), invoice_id nullable
- invoices: client_id, number, issued_on, due_on, status (draft/sent/paid), total_cents

Features in scope:
- Client list and detail page showing projects, unbilled minutes, invoice history
- Kanban board per project, drag tasks between the three statuses
- One global timer: start it from a task, stop it anywhere, it survives a page reload
- Manual time entry editing, including fixing durations after the fact
- Invoice builder: pick a client, it pulls all billable unbilled time, groups by project, applies the client rate, lets me add flat-fee line items, then writes a PDF to disk and marks those entries invoiced
- Dashboard: hours this week, unbilled value, overdue invoices

Explicitly out of scope: authentication, multi-user, roles, Stripe, email sending, telemetry, any cloud service.

Keep config in .env (COMPANY_NAME, COMPANY_ADDRESS, CURRENCY, TAX_RATE) and ship a .env.example. Seed the database with two clients and one project so the UI is not empty on first run. Add an npm script that copies the SQLite file into ./backups with a timestamp. Write a README with exactly the commands needed to run it and nothing else.
